page.after:
What the differences mean

Every figure here is arithmetic from rated numbers, run against one outage load: a fridge, a chest freezer, Wi-Fi, four LED bulbs, two phone chargers and a CPAP, which Lights On Labs puts at about 3,284 Wh a day. The sun figure is StormWatts' mid case: 4.5 peak sun hours × 0.85 charge-path efficiency = 3.825 Wh a day per rated panel watt. Dealectric does not test units.

  • Panel watts that cover the load: 3,284 ÷ 3.825 = 859 W, so about 860 W. Under $4,000, only the kits with 1,000 W or 1,200 W of panels clear it.
  • ALLPOWERS R3500 + 2× SP039: 1,200 × 3.825 = 4,590 Wh a day, 1,306 Wh more than the load. The battery alone holds 3,168 ÷ 3,284 = 0.96 of a day. Its $2,562.15 is the store price read 2026-11-18; our checkout code has been cart-tested on the one-panel kit only.
  • Same station, one panel: 600 × 3.825 = 2,295 Wh, 70% of the load. 3,284 − 2,295 = 989 Wh short, and 3,168 ÷ 989 = 3.2 days. The second panel adds $569.05 at store prices ($2,562.15 − $1,993.10). The SP039 alone was $599.00 the same day, so the two-panel kit costs $29.95 less than the one-panel kit plus a panel.
  • Same station, 400 W panel (SP037): 400 × 3.825 = 1,530 Wh, 47% of the load; 3,168 ÷ 1,754 = 1.8 days, at $1,586.73 through our link ($1,803.10 store price).
  • Anker SOLIX S5000 + 2× 400 W: 800 × 3.825 = 3,060 Wh, 224 Wh short; 5,024 ÷ 224 = about 22 days. For an order placed today, 11–12 weeks lands in early February 2027.
  • BLUETTI Apex 200 + B500K + 2× 500 W: 1,000 × 3.825 = 3,825 Wh, 541 Wh over the load, with 7,680 ÷ 3,284 = 2.3 days in the battery for days without sun. It is under $4,000 only through our link: $3,986.20 against $4,196.00 at the store. The kit was $251 less than the same parts bought separately at BLUETTI on 2026-11-17.
  • BLUETTI Apex 300 + 2× 500 W: the same 1,000 W harvest on a 2,764.8 Wh battery, at $1.13 per Wh. That day the kit cost $102 more than its parts bought separately; the Apex 300 + B300K + 2× 350 W kit cost $101 more than its parts.

StormWatts' 4.5 sun hours is a mid case. Solar Gen Advisor's rule is that winter sun roughly halves the harvest, so here is the same arithmetic with every panel figure halved:

How panel watts turn into outage days

Days = battery Wh ÷ (daily load − panel watts × 3.825). While the panels harvest less than the load, the battery makes up the gap each day and runs down. Once they harvest more, an average day ends with the battery full. That is why 200 W more panel on the same R3500 moves the figure from 1.8 days to 3.2, and a second 600 W panel moves it past the load altogether.

The figure is very sensitive near the line. The S5000 kit's 22 days rests on a 224 Wh daily gap. Andrew Riha (pv magazine USA, 2026-10-28) measured about 10 W of standby draw on the S5000 with the 120 V output on, 5% of charge in 24 hours. That is 240 Wh a day, and the gap becomes 464 Wh: 5,024 ÷ 464 = about 11 days. The battery figures in the table are rated Wh with no inverter loss, so every row is a best case on the same footing.

One measurement supports the 0.85 factor. Riha recorded a 680 W peak from the S5000 kit's own two PS400 panels wired in series on the high-voltage input, on a sunny October day in Northern California: 85% of their 800 W rating. A peak is not a day's average. In a real utility shutoff, the same unit ran a large refrigerator plus phones and small devices for 61.5 hours, from 100% to 18%.

Do the pick's panels fit? ALLPOWERS lists the R3500's solar input as 2,000 W max, XT60, 12–150 V MPPT, 40 A, and the SP039 as a 44 V panel with MC4 leads. Two in series make 88 V, inside 150 V. In parallel, 600 ÷ 44 = 13.6 A each and 27.3 A together, inside 40 A. The pair uses 1,200 W of the 2,000 W limit. The listing gives no open-circuit voltage, which is higher than 44 V, so read the panel label before wiring in series. The two-panel box lists one solar PV connection cable. Each SP039 weighs 27.5 lb.

And the S5000's? Anker lists two inputs: 11–60 V, 17 A, 1,000 W and 16–165 V, 17 A, 2,000 W. The kit's panels are 48 V each, so the series pair (96 V) fits only the 16–165 V input. The kit uses 800 W of a 3,000 W limit, so adding panels later to get past 860 W is possible. Anker gives 32–104°F as the charging temperature, so a unit in an unheated garage takes no solar below freezing.

What the lower price gives up. ALLPOWERS states over 3,500 charging cycles for the R3500 with no capacity end point. BLUETTI states up to 6,000 cycles to 80% capacity for the Apex 300. Anker states up to 10,000 cycles for the S5000, with more than 60% of capacity left.

Where the line was drawn. Every row is a station and its panels sold as one listing at or under $4,000 on the date read; BLUETTI and ALLPOWERS kits from our table are counted at the price through our link. Left out for price: BLUETTI 5kWh RV Kit + 4 × 100 W ($4,084.05 through our link), BLUETTI Apex 300 + B500K + 500 W ($4,179.05) and Anker's S5000 bundles with an expansion battery (from $5,099.99). Anker's F3800 Plus + 400 W kit was sold out on Anker's kit page on 2026-11-18. EcoFlow and Jackery kits are absent because their US stores did not return bundle prices to us on 2026-11-18.

Not recommended

BLUETTI 5kWh RV Kit + 2 × 100 W, for a home outage. At $3,799.05 through our link ($3,999.00 store price) it is the most expensive row that ships now. Its 200 W of panels yield 765 Wh a day, 23% of the load, so its 5,120 Wh lasts about 2.0 days and a refill takes 25.6 full-sun hours at rated output. It is also a fixed system, not a portable station: BLUETTI's box list includes wood screws, anchors and a drilling template. It belongs in an RV build, where its 5,000 W output and alternator wiring pack matter.

400 W kits in general, at this budget. 400 W replaces 47% of the load. The Anker SOLIX F3000 + 400 W lasts about 1.8 days at $0.85 per Wh, a higher price per Wh than six of the other seven rows.
